content: Renal excretion of des-ciclesonide is a minor route of elimination, accounting for less than or equal to 20% of its clearance. In a 12-week study involving children aged 6 to 11 years with perennial allergic rhinitis, des-ciclesonide was detected in 50% of subjects treated with 200 mcg of ciclesonide nasal spray daily and in 5% of those treated with 100 mcg daily. In a separate 6-week study involving children aged 2 to 5 years with perennial allergic rhinitis, des-ciclesonide was detected in 41%, 22%, and 13% of subjects treated with 200 mcg, 100 mcg, and 25 mcg of ciclesonide nasal spray daily, respectively. Drug-Drug Interactions: In vitro studies using human liver microsomes indicate that des-ciclesonide does not exhibit inhibitory or induction effects on the metabolism of other drugs processed by cytochrome P450 enzymes. However, the inhibitory potential of ciclesonide on cytochrome P450 isoenzymes has not been studied. Plasma protein binding of des-ciclesonide was not affected by warfarin or salicylic acid in in vitro studies, suggesting no potential for protein binding-based drug interactions. In a drug interaction study, co-administration of orally inhaled ciclesonide and oral erythromycin, a moderate inhibitor of cytochrome P450 3A4, did not affect the pharmacokinetics of either des-ciclesonide or erythromycin. Nonclinical Toxicology: Ciclesonide showed no carcinogenic potential in a 104-week study in mice at oral doses up to 900 mcg/kg (approximately 20 and 10 times the maximum human daily intranasal dose in adults and children aged 6 to 11 years, respectively, based on mcg/m²) or in a 104-week study in rats at inhalation doses up to 193 mcg/kg (approximately 8 and 5 times the maximum human daily intranasal dose in adults and children aged 6 to 11 years, respectively, based on mcg/m²). Ciclesonide was not mutagenic in an Ames test or a forward mutation assay and was not clastogenic in a human lymphocyte assay or an in vitro micronucleus test. However, it was clastogenic in an in vivo mouse micronucleus test, with similar findings observed for the reference corticosteroid dexamethasone. No evidence of impaired fertility was observed in a reproductive study conducted in male and female rats dosed orally up to 900 mcg/kg/day (approximately 35 times the maximum human daily intranasal dose in adults based on mcg/m²). Reproductive Toxicology Studies: Oral administration of ciclesonide in rats at doses up to 900 mcg/kg (approximately 35 times the maximum human daily dose in adults based on mcg/m²) did not result in teratogenicity or other fetal effects. However, subcutaneous administration of ciclesonide in rabbits at doses of 5 mcg/kg (less than the maximum daily intranasal dose in adults based on mcg/m²) or greater caused fetal toxicity, including fetal loss, reduced fetal weight, cleft palate, skeletal abnormalities (e.g., incomplete ossifications), and skin effects. No toxicity was observed at a dose of 1 mcg/kg (less than the maximum human daily intranasal dose in adults based on mcg/m²). Clinical Studies in Adults and Adolescents (12 Years and Older): The efficacy of OMNARIS Nasal Spray was evaluated in three randomized, double-blind, parallel-group, multicenter, placebo-controlled clinical trials lasting 2 to 6 weeks. These trials were conducted in the United States and Canada and included 1,524 patients (495 males and 1,029 females), of whom 79 were adolescents aged 12 to 17 years. The racial distribution included 1,374 Caucasians, 69 Blacks, 31 Asians, and 50 patients classified as Other. Of the total patients, 546 received OMNARIS Nasal Spray 200 mcg once daily, administered as two sprays in each nostril. Patients enrolled in the studies were aged 12 to 86 years, had a history of seasonal or perennial allergic rhinitis, a positive skin test to at least one relevant allergen, and active symptoms of allergic rhinitis at study entry. Efficacy assessment was based on patient-recorded severity of four nasal symptoms (runny nose, nasal itching, sneezing, and nasal congestion) using a 0-3 categorical severity scale (0 = absent, 1 = mild, 2 = moderate, 3 = severe). Reflective scoring required patients to record symptom severity over the previous 12 hours, while instantaneous scoring required patients to record symptom severity at the time of recording.
